bill.title: Great Lakes Fishery Research Reauthorization Act
bill.officialSummary: Great Lakes Fishery Research Reauthorization Act This act reauthorizes through FY2030 research and monitoring conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey in support of binational fisheries within the Great Lakes Basin. This research is completed through the Great Lakes Science Center and may involve invasive species science, studies on fishery resources, and the use of biological assessment tools and other capabilities to support fishery management decisions.

classification.plainSummary: This bill extends funding authorization through fiscal year 2030 for U.S. Geological Survey research and monitoring programs that support fisheries management in the Great Lakes. The work, conducted through the Great Lakes Science Center, includes studying invasive species, assessing fish populations, and providing scientific tools to help manage the binational fishery. The bill continues an existing program rather than creating new requirements or restrictions.

industries.rationale: Commercial fishing operations in the Great Lakes Basin rely on the fishery management decisions that this research supports.

plain.whatItDoes: This measure would renew through the 2030 budget year research and monitoring conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey in support of binational fisheries within the Great Lakes Basin.
plain.whoItTouches: People who use public land, and people who live beside it.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in what may be done on that land. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
